source_text: Cum ergo furor interdicitur nobis, ab omni spectaculo auferimur, etiam a circo, ubi proprie furor praesidet. aspice populum ad id spectaculum iam cum furore uenientem, iam tumultuosum, iam caecum, iam de sponsionibus concitatum. tardus est illi pr[aetor, semper oculi in urna eius cum sortibus uolutantur. dehinc ad signum anxii pendent, unius dementiae una uox est. cognosce dementiam de uanitate: misit, dicunt et nuntiant inuicem quod simul ab omnibus uisum est. teneo testimonium caecitatis: non uident missum quid sit, mappam putant; sed est diaboli ab alto praecipitati figura. ex eo itaque itur in furias et animos et discordias et quicquid non licet sacerdotibus pacis. inde maledicta, conuicia sine iustitia odii, etiam suffragia sine merito amoris. quid enim suum consecuturi sunt, qui illic agunt, qui sui non sunt? nisi forte hoc solum, per quod sui non sunt: de aliena infelicitate contristantur, de aliena felicitate laetantur. quicquid optant, quicquid abominantur, extraneum ab iis est; ita et amor apud illos otiosus et odium iniustum. an forsitan sine causa amare liceat quam sine causa odisse? deus certe etiam cum causa prohibet odisse, qui inimicos diligi iubet; deus etiam cum causa maledicere non sinit, qui maledicentes benedici praecipit. sed circo quid amarius, ubi ne principibus quidem aut ciuibus suis parcunt? si quid horum, quibus circus furit, alicubi conpetit sanctis, etiam in circo licebit, si uero nusquam, ideo nec. in circo.
thought_title: The circus is the seat of fury, and Christians are removed from it
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that because fury is forbidden to Christians, they are removed from every show, and he now examines the circus as the place where fury properly presides.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, when fury is forbidden to us, we are removed from every show, even from the circus, where fury properly presides. Look at the people coming to that show already with fury, already disorderly, already blind, already stirred up about bets. The praetor is slow for them; their eyes are always rolling in his urn with the lots. Then at the signal they hang in anxiety; there is one voice of one madness. Recognize the madness from the vanity: 'He has sent it,' they say, and they announce to one another what has been seen by all at the same time. I hold the testimony of their blindness: they do not see what the thing sent is; they think it is a napkin; but it is the figure of the devil cast down from on high. And so from that it goes into rages and passions and quarrels and whatever is not permitted to priests of peace. From there come curses, insults without a just cause of hatred, even partisanship without a merit of love. For what of their own are they going to obtain, who act there, who are not their own? Unless perhaps this alone, through which they are not their own: they are saddened by another's misfortune, they rejoice at another's good fortune. Whatever they wish, whatever they detest, is foreign to them; so also love among them is idle and hatred unjust. Or perhaps is it permitted to love without cause more than to hate without cause? God certainly forbids hating even with cause, who commands enemies to be loved; God does not allow cursing even with cause, who commands cursers to be blessed. But what is more bitter than the circus, where they do not spare even princes or their own citizens? If any of these things, by which the circus rages, is fitting for saints anywhere, then it will also be permitted in the circus; but if nowhere, then for that reason not in the circus.

choices.english: we are removed from every show
choices.why: Keeps the passive force of auferimur and the comprehensive omni; 'removed' preserves the sense of being taken away rather than merely abstaining.
rejected: we are taken away from every spectacle
we are kept from all shows

choices.why: Proprie means 'properly' or 'in its own right'; 'presides' keeps the juridical/religious force of praesideo, suggesting fury as the presiding power of the circus.
rejected: where rage is properly in charge

choices.why: Concitatum is passive participle with de + ablative expressing cause; 'stirred up about bets' keeps the causal force and the agitation.

choices.english: there is one voice of one madness
choices.why: The genitive dementiae is kept as 'of one madness' to preserve the rhetorical pairing of unius...una and the idea that the crowd's single voice expresses a single shared madness.
rejected: one voice of a single frenzy
a single voice of one folly

choices.term: mappam putant; sed est diaboli ab alto praecipitati figura
choices.english: they think it is a napkin; but it is the figure of the devil cast down from on high
choices.why: Mappa is the cloth used to start the races; 'napkin' is the literal object. Figura is kept as 'figure' to preserve the typological reading Tertullian gives the mappa as a symbol of the devil's fall.
rejected: they think it is a cloth; but it is the image of the devil thrown down from above
they suppose it is a handkerchief; but it is the shape of the devil cast from on high

choices.why: Keeps the literal sacerdotibus as 'priests' and pacis as 'of peace', preserving the Christian identity Tertullian assigns to believers as ministers of peace.

bible_refs.note: qui inimicos diligi iubet (who commands enemies to be loved) and qui maledicentes benedici praecipit (who commands cursers to be blessed) echo the Lord's command to love enemies and bless those who curse.

pass_b_english: So when fury is forbidden to us, we are removed from every show, even from the circus, where fury properly presides. Look at the crowd coming to that show already with fury, already disorderly, already blind, already stirred up about bets. The praetor is too slow for them; their eyes are always rolling with the lots in his urn. Then they hang anxiously on the signal, and there is one voice of one madness. Recognize the madness from its vanity: "He's off," they say, and they tell each other what everyone has seen at the same moment. I have here the evidence of their blindness: they do not see what has been thrown. They think it is the starting cloth, but it is the figure of the devil cast down from on high. From that, then, they go into furies and passions and quarrels and everything not permitted to priests of peace. From there come curses and insults without any just cause for hatred, even applause without any deserving love. For what will those who act there gain for themselves, when they are not themselves? Unless perhaps this alone, through which they are not themselves: they are saddened by another's misfortune and rejoice at another's good fortune. Whatever they wish for, whatever they detest, is foreign to them; so their love is groundless and their hatred unjust. Or can it be permitted to love without cause any more than to hate without cause? God certainly forbids hatred even with cause, since He commands enemies to be loved; God does not allow cursing even with cause, since He commands those who curse to be blessed. But what is more bitter than the circus, where they do not even spare their rulers or their own citizens? If any of these things in which the circus rages is fitting for the saints anywhere, then it will also be permitted in the circus; but if nowhere, then not in the circus either.

The source says 'ita et amor apud illos otiosus et odium iniustum' — 'otiosus' means idle, at leisure, without purpose. The English 'idle' is a literal rendering, but 'groundless' better matches the parallel with 'unjust' and the preceding 'without cause.' I changed 'idle' to 'groundless.'
